title: Citizens (1791)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Haskalah: Hebrew stretched to talk about telescopes, and Ben Zoma learning from everyone. Your line was enlightenment. What did you learn, and from whom? Today the week closes with a vote. Day nine hundred seventy-three.

A hall in Paris, crowded and loud. The French Revolution has torn up the old order. The new assembly has declared that men are born free and equal in rights. And now a hard question is on the floor: does that include the Jews? Some deputies say yes, obviously. Others say Jews are a separate nation and can never be truly French. The debate goes back and forth, session after session. A people who, all week in this story, have lived behind lines drawn by others are waiting to hear whether a line is about to be erased. Today, one word: citizens.
screen: `FREE AND EQUAL IN RIGHTS.` → `DOES THAT INCLUDE THE JEWS?` → `A LINE ABOUT TO BE ERASED?`

segments.voice: The answer, in the end, was yes. Revolutionary France made Jews full citizens, with the same rights as anyone else: to live where they chose, to work in any trade, to vote. For Jews in France, it changed daily life. But it came with a bargain, and one deputy, Count Stanislas de Clermont-Tonnerre, put it bluntly. Roughly: to the Jews as a nation, nothing; to the Jews as individuals, everything. In other words, you may be equal, one by one, but not as a community that governs itself. Remember the Council of Four Lands, and the Jewish courts and councils that had run Jewish life? Citizenship asked Jews to hand much of that to the state, and to become French citizens of the Jewish faith. Some welcomed that as freedom at last. Others worried about what a people loses when it becomes only a religion. The Torah has its own line about equal law, though there it is a command to Israel about the stranger living among them. In Leviticus, the King James Bible reads: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for one of your own country." In Europe, Jews had long been the strangers. Now a country was offering them one manner of law. And that closes a week of boundaries. A yeshiva that drew students from many places. The Pale, a line drawn around a people. The cantonists, children taken across it. Salanter, working on the self. Mendelssohn and the maskilim, building bridges. And now a vote that opened a door, with a price attached.
screen: `FULL CITIZENS, EQUAL IN RIGHTS.` · `AS INDIVIDUALS, EVERYTHING.` · `ONE MANNER OF LAW.` · then, large: `A DOOR OPENED, WITH A PRICE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: value your citizenship. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Think of one right you have where you live that you rarely think about: to vote, to move, to speak, to worship or not to worship, to go to court. If you're not a citizen where you live, think of one protection you do have there. Let it become concrete: a polling place, a courthouse, a street you walk without asking anyone. Then remember the people in that Paris hall, waiting to hear whether that right was theirs. If you pray, you can give thanks for that right in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Citizens. Revolutionary France made Jews full and equal citizens, as individuals, asking them to become French citizens of the Jewish faith. Today's word.
Your line: citizens. Today, use one right on purpose: read a local notice, write a representative, or simply walk somewhere and remember it's yours to walk. Day nine hundred seventy-three.
